name: Pizza party
seoDesc: Pizza party: work out you should order from the people at the party and the slices per pizza. A free food calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: Supply the people at the party, the slices per pizza and the price and the Pizza party calculator solves for you should order. It suits portioning, timing or nutrition. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Pizza party calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pizza party calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports you should order in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the size, the crust and the type); then you type in the people at the party, the slices per pizza and the price.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A plain number with no unit attached.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as moderately hungry, hungry and starving. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as small (10"), medium (12") and large (14"). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as thin and classic. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 5 options, such as veggie pizza, cheese pizza and pepperoni pizza. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.

4 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pizza party calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

You should order=(rounded up, (we are... × people at the party ÷ (slices per pizza × (crust, type, pizza diameter, slices per pizza))))
Slices per person=(slices per pizza × (rounded up, (we are... × people at the party ÷ (slices per pizza × (crust, type, pizza diameter, slices per pizza)))) ÷ people at the party)
Total cost=(price × (rounded up, (we are... × people at the party ÷ (slices per pizza × (crust, type, pizza diameter, slices per pizza)))))
Cost per person=((price × (rounded up, (we are... × people at the party ÷ (slices per pizza × (crust, type, pizza diameter, slices per pizza))))) ÷ people at the party)
Calories per slice=(crust, type, pizza diameter, slices per pizza)
Each person will eat=((crust, type, pizza diameter, slices per pizza) × (slices per pizza × (rounded up, (we are... × people at the party ÷ (slices per pizza × (crust, type, pizza diameter, slices per pizza)))) ÷ people at the party))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — We are set to hungry, Size set to small (10"), Slices per pizza = 8 and Crust set to Classic — it reports Pizza diameter = 1000 cm.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Pizza diameter = 1000 cm should be roughly the size you expected from We are set to hungry and Size set to small (10").

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pizza party calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Working out timing so everything finishes together
  • Scaling a recipe up or down
  • Checking portions before you shop
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the people at the party, the slices per pizza and the price — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Pizza party calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns you should order, derived from the people at the party, the slices per pizza and the price. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pizza party calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the people at the party, the slices per pizza and the price, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter pizza diameter in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Pizza diameter opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Pizza diameter = 1000 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pizza party calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
